title: The Thing About My Folks
full_review:
Here's a film with its heart in the right place, to be sure, and it gives Peter Falk a terrific vehicle for his latter-day emoting, but the well-intentioned "The Thing About My Folks" (Picturehouse) is, alas, dramatically lackluster, a not-very-compelling father-son bonding movie.

Sam Kleinman (Falk), the irascible dad, finds himself suddenly and mysteriously abandoned by his wife, Muriel (Olympia Dukakis), and shows up utterly befuddled on his son Ben's (Paul Reiser) doorstep.

Leaving his wife (Elizabeth Perkins) and two young girls behind in New York City, Ben and the old codger take to the road where they survey farm property, attend a local baseball game, play pool, instigate a barroom brawl, dine with a flirtatious mother and daughter, and ponder the constellations. Throughout it all, they hammer out the past and come to a greater understanding of their current relationship.

Near the start of their trip, Ben produces a never-delivered letter he stole from his mother's dresser as a child. In that letter, Muriel outlined Sam's insensitivities to her, and announced she was going to leave him. She didn't, but the reasons she articulated in that decades-old letter (mostly that Sam was too preoccupied with his job to give her attention) seem to mirror the reasons she walked out on him now.

Director Raymond De Felitta's sentimental and talky film has some truisms with which everyone will empathize, but despite good performances -- when Dukakis appears late in the film, she's outstanding, too -- and several touching moments, the pacing is sluggish. Reiser's script, though sometimes true to life, is mostly self-consciously contrived.

Four-letter words spill from Sam's lips in unceasing profusion, necessitating a far more restrictive classification than a basically sweet-natured, life-affirming film like this -- with its strong pro-family message, underscored with forgiveness -- should receive.

The film contains considerable profanity, rough and crude language and humor, a violent episode and sexual innuendo. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
